::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- choose between `geom_bar()` (R counts for you) and `geom_col()` (you supply the heights);
- **order** bars meaningfully with `forcats`, and draw readable **horizontal** bars;
- show two categorical variables with **stacked, dodged and proportional** bars, and pick the right one for the question;
- add **labels** to bars;
- explain why **pie charts** and **bar charts of means** ("dynamite plots") are usually poor choices, and what to use instead.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)
```
:::


## 1. Why bar charts?

A **bar chart** is the picture of a frequency table (see [Frequency tables](../05-descriptive/21-frequency-tables.qmd)): one bar per category, with a length proportional to a number — usually a count or a proportion. It works so well because we compare **lengths from a common baseline** very accurately.

Two different situations need two different geoms:

| You have… | Use | What ggplot2 does |
|---|---|---|
| One row per **observation** (e.g., one row per car) | `geom_bar()` | counts the rows in each category (`stat = "count"`) |
| One row per **category**, with the height already computed (a count, a mean, a percentage) | `geom_col()` | draws the values as they are (`stat = "identity"`) |

## 2. Counting with `geom_bar()`

How many cars in `mtcars` have 4, 6 or 8 cylinders?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "Number of cars")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Number of cars by number of cylinders.](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-bar-basic-1.png){#fig-bar-basic fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


`factor(cyl)` treats cylinders as categories. We never computed the counts: `geom_bar()` did it.

Setting (not mapping) `fill` and `alpha` changes the look of all bars; mapping `fill` to the same variable as `x` colours each bar differently but adds no information, so we remove the legend:


::: {#fig-bar-fill .cell layout-ncol="2" layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "Number of cars")

ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), fill = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar() +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "Number of cars")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![fill and alpha set](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-bar-fill-1.png){#fig-bar-fill-1 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![fill mapped, legend removed](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-bar-fill-2.png){#fig-bar-fill-2 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

Left: a constant fill colour with transparency. Right: fill mapped to the x variable — colourful, but redundant.
:::


## 3. Precomputed values with `geom_col()`

Often you first summarise with `dplyr` and then plot the result. The same counts as above, computed explicitly:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cyl_counts <- mtcars |>
  count(cyl) |>
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl))
cyl_counts
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   cyl  n
#> 1   4 11
#> 2   6  7
#> 3   8 14
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(cyl_counts, aes(x = cyl, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "Number of cars")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The same chart from a summary table, with geom_col().](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-col-1.png){#fig-col fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


Using `geom_bar()` on `cyl_counts` would be a mistake: it would count the **rows** of the summary table (one per category) and draw three bars of height 1.

## 4. Order matters

For a **nominal** variable the alphabetical order of the bars is arbitrary and makes comparisons harder. Sort the bars **by frequency** with `forcats::fct_infreq()`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
states <- tibble(division = state.division)

ggplot(states, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(division)))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of states", y = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Number of US states in each census division, ordered by frequency, with horizontal bars for readable labels.](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-order-1.png){#fig-order fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


Three things happen here:

1. `fct_infreq()` orders the levels from most to least frequent;
2. `fct_rev()` reverses that order, because ggplot2 draws the first level at the **bottom** of a vertical axis — so the largest bar ends up on top;
3. mapping the variable to `y` gives **horizontal bars**, which leave plenty of room for long category names. (The older way is to map `x` and add `coord_flip()`; both work.)

When the heights are precomputed, use `fct_reorder()` to order a factor by another variable:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
feed_means <- chickwts |>
  summarise(mean_weight = mean(weight), n = n(), .by = feed)

ggplot(feed_means, aes(x = mean_weight, y = fct_reorder(feed, mean_weight))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Mean weight after 6 weeks (g)", y = "Feed")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Mean chick weight by feed type, ordered by the mean.](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-reorder-1.png){#fig-reorder fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


**Do not reorder ordinal variables** (education level, agreement scales, age classes, months): their natural order carries information. Keep the level order and, if needed, set it with `factor(..., levels = ...)`.

## 5. Adding labels

Labels with the exact values help when readers need the numbers. On a summary table, map `label` and nudge the text above the bars:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(cyl_counts, aes(cyl, n)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4) +
  expand_limits(y = max(cyl_counts$n) * 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "Number of cars")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Counts written above the bars.](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-labels-1.png){#fig-labels fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


`vjust = -0.4` moves the text just above the top of each bar, and `expand_limits()` leaves room so that the highest label is not cut off. With `geom_bar()` the counts exist only inside the plot; refer to them with `after_stat()`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(penguins, aes(island)) +
  geom_bar(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of penguins")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Labels on a geom_bar() chart via after_stat(count).](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-labels-stat-1.png){#fig-labels-stat fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


For horizontal bars, use `hjust` instead of `vjust`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mpg_by_cyl <- mtcars |>
  summarise(mean_mpg = mean(mpg), .by = cyl) |>
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl))

ggplot(mpg_by_cyl, aes(x = mean_mpg, y = cyl)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_mpg, 1)), hjust = -0.15) +
  expand_limits(x = max(mpg_by_cyl$mean_mpg) * 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Mean miles per gallon", y = "Cylinders")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Mean fuel economy by cylinders, horizontal bars with rounded labels.](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-labels-horizontal-1.png){#fig-labels-horizontal fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


(We will come back to bars of **means** in Section 8 — they have a serious problem.)

## 6. Two categorical variables

How is the transmission type (`am`: automatic or manual) distributed across cylinder classes? First we turn the codes into labelled factors:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cars <- mtcars |>
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl),
         am = factor(am, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("automatic", "manual")))
```
:::


The `position` argument decides how the bars of the second variable are arranged:


::: {#fig-positions .cell layout-ncol="3" layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = cyl, fill = am)) +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", fill = "Transmission")

p + geom_bar() + labs(y = "Number of cars")
p + geom_bar(position = position_dodge(preserve = "single")) +
  labs(y = "Number of cars")
p + geom_bar(position = "fill") + labs(y = "Proportion")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Stacked (default)](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-positions-1.png){#fig-positions-1 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Dodged](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-positions-2.png){#fig-positions-2 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Filled (proportions)](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-positions-3.png){#fig-positions-3 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

Three arrangements of the same counts.
:::


| Arrangement | Answers best | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| **Stacked** | Totals per category, plus a rough split | Only the bottom segment shares a baseline; the others are hard to compare |
| **Dodged** | Compare counts of the subgroups directly | Totals are harder to see |
| **Filled** (`position = "fill"`) | Compare **conditional proportions** across categories | Hides how many observations are behind each bar |

The filled chart is the picture of the conditional distribution from [Describing two variables](../05-descriptive/23-two-variables.qmd): within each cylinder class, the proportion of automatic and manual cars. It shows clearly that 86% of 8-cylinder cars are automatic. Put the **explanatory** variable on the x axis and the **response** in the fill — just as you would compute percentages within the categories of the explanatory variable.

`position_dodge(preserve = "single")` keeps all bars the same width even when a combination is missing — important for data such as island × species in `penguins`, which has empty cells.

### Proportional bars with percentage labels

To label a filled chart, compute the proportions yourself and use `position_fill(vjust = 0.5)` to centre the labels inside the segments:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
island_species <- penguins |>
  count(island, species) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n), .by = island)

island_n <- count(penguins, island)

ggplot(island_species, aes(x = island, y = prop, fill = species)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(prop, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5), colour = "white") +
  geom_text(data = island_n, aes(x = island, y = 1.04,
                                 label = paste0("n = ", n)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion", fill = "Species")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Species composition of each island, with percentages and group sizes.](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-fill-labels-1.png){#fig-fill-labels fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


Writing $n$ above each bar fixes the main weakness of proportional bars: Torgersen's 100% Adelie is based on 52 birds, Biscoe's figures on 168.

### Mosaic plots

A **mosaic plot** goes one step further: bar *widths* are proportional to the size of each group, so the **area** of each rectangle is proportional to the count in that cell. Base R draws one directly from a table:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mosaicplot(table(penguins$island, penguins$species),
           main = "", xlab = "Island", ylab = "Species",
           color = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Mosaic plot of island by species: column widths reflect the number of birds per island.](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-mosaic-1.png){#fig-mosaic fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


(For a ggplot2 version, see the `ggmosaic` package.)

## 7. Why pie charts are usually worse

A pie chart shows proportions as **angles and areas** of slices. Humans judge angles and areas much less accurately than lengths on a common scale. Compare the same six counts:


::: {#fig-pie .cell layout-ncol="2" layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(chickwts, aes(x = "", fill = feed)) +
  geom_bar(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(fill = "Feed")

ggplot(chickwts, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(feed)))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of chicks", y = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Pie chart](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-pie-1.png){#fig-pie-1 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Bar chart](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-pie-2.png){#fig-pie-2 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

The number of chicks per feed type as a pie chart and as a bar chart. Which feed has the most chicks?
:::


In the pie it is almost impossible to say whether soybean or casein is larger, or which slices are equal; in the bar chart it is immediate (14 soybean chicks, three feeds with 12 each). Pies also need a colour legend, and they fail completely for comparing two groups side by side. A pie can be acceptable for **two or three** parts of a whole with very different sizes; otherwise use bars. Never use 3-D pies: perspective distorts the slices.

The pie is built with the grammar of graphics too: a single stacked bar (`x = ""`) drawn in polar coordinates (`coord_polar(theta = "y")`).

## 8. Bars for means: the "dynamite plot" problem

A very common chart in scientific papers shows the **mean** of each group as a bar with an **error bar** on top, usually the mean ± one **standard error** (SE). The SE measures how precisely a sample mean estimates the population mean: $\text{SE} = s / \sqrt{n}$ (you will learn exactly why in [Sampling distributions](../07-probability/30-sampling-distributions.qmd)).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
feed_summary <- chickwts |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(weight),
            se = sd(weight) / sqrt(n),
            .by = feed)
feed_summary
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>        feed  n  mean    se
#> 1 horsebean 10 160.2 12.21
#> 2   linseed 12 218.8 15.08
#> 3   soybean 14 246.4 14.47
#> 4 sunflower 12 328.9 14.10
#> 5  meatmeal 11 276.9 19.57
#> 6    casein 12 323.6 18.60
```


:::
:::



::: {#fig-dynamite .cell layout-ncol="2" layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(feed_summary, aes(feed, mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weight (g)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

ggplot(chickwts, aes(feed, weight)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "pointrange",
               colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weight (g)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Dynamite plot](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-dynamite-1.png){#fig-dynamite-1 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Data, mean and ± 1 SE](26-categorical-plots_files/figure-html/fig-dynamite-2.png){#fig-dynamite-2 fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::

Left: the classic 'dynamite plot' (bar = mean, whisker = ± 1 SE). Right: the same means and SEs drawn over the individual chicks.
:::


What is wrong with the dynamite plot?

1. **It hides the data.** With 10–14 chicks per group, the full data fit on the plot. The bars say nothing about spread, skewness, outliers or $n$; very different datasets give identical dynamite plots.
2. **The bar suggests the data go from 0 to the mean.** For counts a bar from zero is natural; for a mean it implies that all values are inside the bar, while in reality about half of them are above it.
3. **The error bar is ambiguous.** Readers rarely know whether it is ± 1 SD, ± 1 SE or a 95% confidence interval — three very different things. Always state it in the caption.
4. **± 1 SE is not a range for the data.** It describes the uncertainty of the *mean*, not where individual observations lie (most chicks are far outside the error bars on the right).

Better alternatives: points with jitter plus mean ± SE (right panel), boxplots with points, or violins (see [Plotting distributions](25-distribution-plots.qmd)). `mean_se()` is a ggplot2 helper that returns the mean and mean ± 1 SE for `stat_summary()`.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: SD, SE and confidence intervals

For a group with $n$ observations, mean $\bar x$ and standard deviation $s$:

- $\bar x \pm s$ describes the **spread of the observations**;
- $\bar x \pm s/\sqrt n$ (± 1 SE) describes the **uncertainty of the mean**; it shrinks as $n$ grows;
- $\bar x \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1} \cdot s/\sqrt n$ is a **95% confidence interval** for the population mean (about $\bar x \pm 2\,\text{SE}$ for moderate $n$); see [Confidence intervals](../08-inference/32-confidence-intervals.qmd).

In `stat_summary()`, `fun.data = mean_cl_normal` (which needs the `Hmisc` package) gives t-based 95% intervals, and `mean_se(mult = 2)` gives mean ± 2 SE.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **`geom_bar()` on a summary table.** It counts rows (all bars of height 1). Use `geom_col()` when you already have the heights.
2. **Alphabetical order for nominal categories.** Order by frequency (`fct_infreq()`) or by value (`fct_reorder()`); keep the natural order for ordinal variables.
3. **Bars that do not start at zero.** A bar's length *is* the value; cutting the axis exaggerates differences. (If zero is irrelevant, use points instead of bars.)
4. **Stacked bars for comparing subgroups.** Only the bottom segment has a common baseline; use dodged or filled bars.
5. **Proportional bars without $n$.** 100% of 3 is not the same as 100% of 300.
6. **Dynamite plots.** Bars of means with error bars hide the data; show the points, and say what the error bars are.
:::

## 9. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. You have a data frame with one row per country and a column `population`. Which geom draws one bar per country with height equal to the population?

`geom_col()` with `aes(x = country, y = population)` — the heights are already in the data. `geom_bar()` would count rows (one per country) and draw bars of height 1.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. You want to show whether the proportion of smokers differs across five age groups. Stacked, dodged or filled bars?

Filled bars (`position = "fill"`) with age group on the x axis and smoking status as fill: they show the conditional proportions directly. Keep the age groups in their natural order and write $n$ on each bar.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. Give two reasons why a dot plot of the data with mean ± SE is better than a bar of the mean with an error bar.

It shows the distribution and the number of observations (spread, skewness, outliers are visible), and it does not suggest that the values lie between zero and the mean. (It also makes clear that ± SE describes the mean, not the data.)
:::

## 10. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — ordered horizontal bars.** Draw a horizontal bar chart of the number of chicks per `feed` in `chickwts`, with the most frequent feed on top.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_26_1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_26_1
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
ggplot(chickwts, aes(y = ______(______(feed)))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of chicks", y = NULL)
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_26_1"}
`fct_infreq()` sorts by frequency; `fct_rev()` reverses the order so that the largest bar is at the top.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_26_1"}
```r
ggplot(chickwts, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(feed)))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of chicks", y = NULL)
```
Soybean has the most chicks (14); horsebean the fewest (10).
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — debug.** This code should draw the mean `len` per supplement type in `ToothGrowth`, but all bars have height 1. Fix it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_26_2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_26_2
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
tg_means <- ToothGrowth |>
  summarise(mean_len = mean(len), .by = supp)

ggplot(tg_means, aes(x = supp)) +
  geom_bar()
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_26_2"}
The heights are already computed in `mean_len`. Which geom uses precomputed heights, and what must be mapped to `y`?
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_26_2"}
```r
ggplot(tg_means, aes(x = supp, y = mean_len)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Supplement", y = "Mean tooth length")
```
`geom_bar()` counted the rows of `tg_means` (one per supplement). With `geom_col()` and `y = mean_len` the bars show the means (about 20.7 for orange juice, `OJ`, and 17.0 for ascorbic acid, `VC`). Even better: show the 30 observations per group with points, as in Section 8.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — conditional proportions.** Using `penguins`, draw filled bars showing the proportion of females and males within each species (exclude birds with unknown sex). Is the sex ratio balanced?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_26_3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_26_3
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
penguins |>
  filter(______) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(position = ______) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion", fill = "Sex")
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_26_3"}
Filter with `!is.na(sex)` and use `position = "fill"`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_26_3"}
```r
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Proportion", fill = "Sex")
```
In every species the split is very close to 50/50 — the researchers sampled pairs of birds.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — replace a dynamite plot.** For `PlantGrowth` (plant `weight` by `group`), draw jittered points with the group mean ± 1 SE on top. Then answer: do the error bars show where most plants are?


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_26_4'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_26_4
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(PlantGrowth, aes(group, weight)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = ______, geom = "pointrange", colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Dried weight (g)",
       caption = "Orange: mean ± 1 standard error")
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_26_4"}
The ggplot2 helper that returns the mean and mean ± 1 SE is `mean_se`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_26_4"}
```r
ggplot(PlantGrowth, aes(group, weight)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "pointrange", colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Dried weight (g)",
       caption = "Orange: mean ± 1 standard error")
```
No: many plants lie well outside the error bars. The SE describes the precision of each **mean** (with 10 plants per group), not the spread of the plants. The caption saying what the error bars are is essential.
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — hair and eye colour.** Convert `HairEyeColor` to a data frame with `as.data.frame()` (columns `Hair`, `Eye`, `Sex`, `Freq`). Draw (a) dodged bars of the counts of eye colour for each hair colour, (b) filled bars of the proportions, with percentage labels. Use `geom_col()` because the counts are in `Freq`. Which chart shows best that blond people mostly have blue eyes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
hec <- as.data.frame(HairEyeColor) |>
  summarise(n = sum(Freq), .by = c(Hair, Eye)) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n), .by = Hair)

ggplot(hec, aes(Hair, n, fill = Eye)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(y = "Number of students")

ggplot(hec, aes(Hair, prop, fill = Eye)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(prop, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5), size = 3) +
  labs(y = "Proportion within hair colour")
```
The filled chart shows the conditional distribution directly: about 74% of blond students have blue eyes. The fill colours here are the course's Okabe–Ito palette; for eye colours you might prefer `scale_fill_manual()` with intuitive colours (keeping them distinguishable).
:::
:::

## Summary

| Goal | ggplot2 |
|---|---|
| Counts from raw data | `geom_bar()` |
| Precomputed heights | `geom_col()` |
| Order by frequency / by value | `fct_infreq(x)`, `fct_reorder(x, value)`; `fct_rev()` to reverse |
| Horizontal bars | map the category to `y` (or `coord_flip()`) |
| Stacked / dodged / filled | `position = "stack"` / `position_dodge(preserve = "single")` / `"fill"` |
| Value labels | `geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4)`; with `geom_bar()`: `stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count))` |
| Labels in filled bars | `geom_text(..., position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5))` |
| Mosaic plot | `mosaicplot(table(a, b))` |
| Mean ± SE over data | `geom_jitter()` + `stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "pointrange")` |

- Bars compare **lengths from zero**: they must start at zero.
- **Order** nominal bars by size; keep ordinal categories in their natural order.
- For two variables, **filled bars** show conditional proportions — add $n$.
- Prefer bars to **pie charts**.
- Do not hide data behind **bars of means**: show the observations and say what error bars represent.
